title: Rolling Updates & Rollbacks 🔄
description: Update your application image without downtime and undo bad changes.

slides.title: The Need for Zero‑Downtime Updates 🚦
slides.content:
# Users hate downtime

If you delete all Pods and then create new ones, your app is unavailable. A **rolling update** replaces Pods gradually, ensuring some instances are always serving traffic.

Kubernetes Deployments offer this by default.

slides.title: Triggering a Rolling Update 🎬
slides.content:
## Change the image

The easiest trigger is updating the container image. You can do it imperatively:
```bash
kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deploy nginx=nginx:1.26
```
Or declaratively: edit `deploy.yaml` and apply.

Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet, starts new Pods, and terminates old ones.

quizData.question: Which command updates the image of a Deployment named 'api'?
quizData.explanation: `kubectl set image` is the dedicated subcommand for updating images.

slides.title: The Rolling Update Process 🎢
slides.content:
## Step by step

1. A new ReplicaSet is created with the updated Pod template.
2. New Pods are started (up to `maxSurge` extra Pods).
3. Once new Pods are Ready, some old Pods are terminated (up to `maxUnavailable`).
4. Repeat until the desired replicas are all new Pods.
5. The old ReplicaSet is scaled down to 0.

You can watch the rollout with:
```bash
kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deploy
```

slides.title: Watch a Rollout
slides.codeSnippet:
kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deploy
# Also see history:
kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-deploy

quizData.question: How do you check if a rolling update is complete?
quizData.explanation: `rollout status` blocks until the rollout is complete or fails.

slides.title: Rolling Back a Bad Update ⏪
slides.content:
## Undo the mistake

If the new version has a bug, you can rollback to the previous revision:
```bash
kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deploy
```
This goes back to the previous ReplicaSet.

To rollback to a specific revision:
```bash
kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deploy --to-revision=2
```
You can see available revisions with `kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-deploy`.

slides.title: Rollback Example
slides.content: If the latest update breaks things, instantly revert:
slides.codeSnippet:
kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deploy
# Wait for it:
kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deploy

quizData.question: Which command reverts a Deployment to the previous revision?
quizData.explanation: `kubectl rollout undo` is the correct subcommand.

slides.title: Revision Limits 📚
slides.content:
## How many old ReplicaSets are kept?

By default, Kubernetes keeps the 10 most recent ReplicaSets (controlled by `spec.revisionHistoryLimit`). Older ones are deleted. Adjust this if you need a longer audit trail.

```yaml
spec:
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
```

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use `--record` (deprecated but useful)

In older versions, `kubectl apply --record` recorded the command in the revision history. Now, the Deployment records the change automatically in its annotations.
